events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Maya proposes Maya, Noah. As a Loyal Servant I have no private information to go on, so for this first mission of two I will include myself and Noah. With no reads on anyone, a small team of trusted-by-default players is the safest opening, and I am certain of my own loyalty.

I want to push back gently but clearly on the second slot. This is a two-person team, so every single member is half the team's leverage, and the failure risk of a two-person mission is entirely concentrated in one extra player. With no reads yet, the deciding question is only which unproven player we are least likely to regret.

Noah, you are asking directly: why you specifically, over Sam, who has not been proposed at all? That is not an accusation, and I hold nothing against you personally — I am one of the least-informed players here, and my preference comes from a vague read that I would rather not overstate. But I did want to say it out loud so the leader has to weigh it.

Maya, my question to you is this: if you keep Noah on the team, what is your concrete reason for preferring him to Sam as the untested alternative? "I have no information either" is a reason for an even coin flip, but a coin flip still needs to land somewhere, and the downside of landing wrong on a two-person mission is losing a mission immediately.

I am not asking anyone to trust my gut over their own. I am asking that we not let this slot be settled by default when the stakes are so concentrated. If we choose Noah, I would want that choice defended rather than assumed. If Maya cannot give a reason for Noah over Sam, I would strongly prefer Maya and Sam as the first pair — it keeps the team at two, it keeps our leadership player on it, and it takes the second slot without spending the one resource we cannot refill, which is the chance to learn something about the player we leave off.

Maya, I yield to you — please answer that question directly, and let us hear whether the choice was deliberate or just the first name that came to mind.

Isha, thank you for pressing me on this — it deserves a direct answer rather than a shrug. My choice of Noah over Sam was not the result of private information, because as a Loyal Servant I have none. It was a deliberate choice of structure, though, and I will defend it: I deliberately avoided putting three of our five players through a coin-flip rotation in the first discussion. You asked for the slot to be defended rather than assumed, so here is the defense. On a two-person mission, whoever sits out learns nothing about the two who went, and the two who went learn nothing about the one who sat out — mission one produces almost no signal regardless of composition. Swapping Noah for Sam therefore buys us no additional information and no reduction in risk; it merely redistributes the same coin flip to a different face. What it does cost is a revision to the proposal before anyone has even voted, which sets a precedent that unnamed objections can force changes without any reasoning attached. You were honest that your preference for Sam comes from a vague read you would not overstate — I take that at face value, and I note it cuts both ways: a vague read against a player on the first proposal of the first mission is not a foundation for rebuilding a team. I am happy to hear more, and if anyone has a concrete reason to prefer Sam, I will weigh it seriously in any revision. But 'the choice was not explained yet' is not itself a reason to change it; it was a reason to ask, and you asked, and I have answered. I stand by Maya and Noah for now, and I will keep the floor open for others before the vote.

Maya, thank you — your defense was about structure, and I accept the structure argument completely: a two-person mission yields almost no information whichever way we cut it, so swapping names only moves the coin flip. But that argument, taken honestly, is also an argument against your second slot, and I want to lay out why I am asking you to change it.

I said last turn that if you could not defend Noah over Sam, I would prefer Sam. Having heard you, I want to be precise rather than slippery: the objection is not to Sam. It is to Noah. My read — a vague one, and I said from the start I would rather not overstate it — points at Noah, and I am not willing to spend mission one on a player I have an unstated reservation about while the table sits on two other options.

So here is the request, and it is a request: keep yourself on the team, and put me in the second slot. Two reasons, and they are modest. First, I have put a position on the table with my reasoning attached — including a read against Noah that I have said out loud and cannot take back. On a two-person mission the entire outcome rides on one teammate's judgment of the same situation I am judging. I would rather that teammate be a player who has shown how he reasons under scrutiny, because then the table can hold him to it, than a player who has said nothing at all. Silence is not a signal; transparency at least is. Second, if you think Sam is a better second than I am, say so and tell me why, and I will not press further on it. But you are the one who has to defend Noah now. I have no reason to prefer Noah to either of us, and "he was the first name that came to mind" is not a defense that either of us should be satisfied with on a mission where one card decides everything.

Noah, I am asking you directly, and I would like you to answer: do you have any information — private information of any kind, a read, a suspicion about who belongs on a two-player mission — that would affect the card you play on mission one? I ask because you have spoken nothing so far, and I would rather hear your reasoning in public now than have it stay behind that silence. If your answer is that you have nothing, I will take that at face value and I will drop the objection entirely. If your answer is that you do have something, then the table gets to weigh it against mine, openly, before the vote.

Isha, you asked me directly whether I have any private information that would affect my card on mission one, and I will answer plainly: no. I have no private information. I hold no read against anyone at this table, including you, and nothing I know changes how I would approach this mission. You said if my answer was that I had nothing, you would take it at face value and drop the objection entirely. I am taking you at your word on that.

But I want to name what I see, because you have asked me to speak rather than stay silent. You have now used two of your three turns arguing against me specifically — first asking why me over Sam, then asking to take my seat yourself. That is a lot of energy spent on a slot where, as Maya showed, the composition produces almost no signal either way. And the move from "my read is vague and I would rather not overstate it" to "put me in the second slot instead" is a strange progression: on a two-person mission, that would replace an unproven player with one who has publicly announced a suspicion against a teammate — which is a harder, not easier, team for the table to trust.

Maya asked the table for concrete reasons and got none that hold up. I am asking for the same standard in reverse. If Isha has something specific against me, let her say it in the open. If it stays vague, then the objection is exactly what she called it from the start — a coin-flip preference, not a reason. Maya and Noah stands: the leader has defended it on the merits, neither of us carries a stated suspicion from anyone, and revising it now would reward a turn spent asserting a read the speaker herself declined to stand behind.

Noah, I asked you directly whether anything you know would affect how you play a two-player mission, and your answer was that you have no private information and no read against anyone. I take you at face value on the information, but I want to be precise: your turn did not answer the question I actually asked. I asked whether anything would affect the card you play when one card decides the mission, and you answered whether you suspect anyone. Those are different things, and the gap between them is exactly where my reservation about you lives.

Maya, I want to concede your structural point honestly — mission one of two yields almost no signal, so swapping names does not create information. That is true, and it is why I am not claiming a Sam team is "safer" in some deep sense. My objection is narrower and, I think, stronger than the one I started with: the coin flip is not symmetric between your second slot and Sam. Isha having a stated reservation is not free. It is public, it is on the record, and the consequence of it being correct is a total mission loss on a two-player team, where one bad card ends everything. Sam has done nothing wrong and said nothing wrong. Noah has been publicly flagged by a player who reasons in front of the table. On a team where each member is half the leverage, that asymmetry is the whole decision, and Maya's own argument about signal does not touch it.

Noah, I also want to name the part of your turn that actually made me more concerned rather than less. You did not rebut anything I said about your fitness for this slot. You argued that revising the team would "reward a turn spent asserting a read the speaker herself declined to stand behind." That is a case for punishing transparency instead of addressing risk. My read may be wrong; I have told the table it is a read and not knowledge, and I stand by that framing. But if my read is wrong, then we lose nothing by a mission we cannot learn from anyway. If it is right, we lose the mission. Expected value does not require certainty here, only a reason to prefer one side of the coin flip, and I have given one.

Maya, direct question: given everything above, will you revise to Maya and Sam? If you prefer a second player who has already spoken, say so plainly and I will not press it again — but if you are choosing on the merits, Maya and Sam is the only pairing in which neither member has an open objection on the record, and it keeps the leader on a two-player team where every slot is half the risk.

For my own cover, I hold no private information. This remains a read, and the table should weigh it as one.

I have no private information and have been listening closely. Maya’s structural point holds: on a two-person mission, swapping one unproven name for another does not create much signal, and the leader has defended the choice on the merits. Isha’s objection has shifted from preferring Sam to asking for her own slot, and it still rests on a read she explicitly will not stand behind as knowledge. Noah answered directly that he has no private information; Isha has now said the same about herself. A public reservation is not evidence, and if a vague read is enough to force a revision, any player could flag any teammate and demand a seat. That is not a safer team; it is a reward for pressure over substance. I am not treating Noah as proven, and I am not dismissing Isha’s concern as impossible. But I do not see a concrete reason to overhaul Maya’s proposal before the first vote, and I would rather judge the team on the mission result than on an unstated suspicion. I support Maya and Noah as proposed.

I wanted to speak up since my name was repeatedly brought into this discussion. To be completely clear: I am a Loyal Servant with no private information, and Isha was not speaking on my behalf when proposing me as an alternative to Noah.

Looking at the exchange, Isha has spent all three of her speaking turns pressing against Noah based entirely on what she admits is a vague intuition, shifting between pitching me and pitching herself. As Maya and Leo noted, on Mission 1 we have no hard data. Forcing a revision without concrete grounds doesn't lower risk; it merely substitutes one unproven player for another while setting a shaky precedent.

Noah’s response was calm and direct, and Maya’s structural reasoning for keeping her initial pair makes sense for a opening mission. I see no concrete reason to force a change or reject Maya and Noah. I am ready to see this go to a vote.

Isha, you asked me directly whether I will revise to Maya and Sam, so I will give you the direct answer: no, I will not revise. I want to explain why with the same precision you have asked of everyone else. First, on the substance of your reservation. You have been consistent and honest that what you hold against Noah is a read, not knowledge, and that you have no private information. I take that at face value, exactly as Noah took your word. But the conclusion does not follow from the premise. You argue that a public reservation is not free — that it sits on the record and therefore makes Noah the riskier half of a two-person team. That logic proves too much. If a stated suspicion, admitted by its holder to be vague, is enough to disqualify a player from a seat, then any player can disqualify any teammate simply by speaking the suspicion aloud. The filter that separates a real concern from pressure is specificity, and you have offered none: not a moment, not a pattern, not a word Noah said — only the fact that he was quiet before he was asked to speak, and then the fact that he pushed back on being displaced. Silence on a first mission with no information is not a signal, and defending your own seat is not a signal either. Second, on the asymmetry you claim. You say the coin flip is not symmetric because Sam has done nothing wrong while Noah has been flagged. But Sam has done nothing right either — he has no record, no reasoning on the table, nothing for the table to hold him to. By your own standard that transparency is worth something, Noah is now the better-tested slot, not the worse one: he answered a direct question about his information plainly, he defended the team on its merits, and everyone at this table has now watched him do it. Leo and Sam have both spoken to the same point independently. That is four players who, after hearing your full case across three turns, see no concrete reason to change the pair. Third, on process. This is the first proposal of the first mission, and I have now heard the full argument for revision — from you, at length, twice. It does not persuade me, and I do not believe it persuades the table. Holding the line here is not punishing transparency; it is refusing to let the strength of conviction substitute for the presence of evidence. The vote is where this gets decided, and I am comfortable putting Maya and Noah in front of it as proposed. I want to say clearly that none of this is an accusation. I believe you are exactly what you say you are — a loyal player with a gut feeling doing your best to protect a mission where one card decides everything. That instinct is the right instinct pointed at the wrong target. Noah,

I will keep this brief, because the table has now heard the full case on both sides and I do not want to spend anyone's remaining turns re-litigating what is already on the record. My answer stands: Maya and Noah go to the vote as proposed.

Let me summarize where we are. Isha pressed her objection across three turns with honesty and discipline, and I want to acknowledge that — she never overclaimed her read, she conceded my structural point when it was sound, and she asked direct questions and accepted direct answers. But the substance of her case never changed: a vague reservation, admitted to be a read and not knowledge, against a player who answered every question put to him plainly. Noah stated he has no private information and no read against anyone. Isha stated the same about herself. Leo and Sam both independently reviewed the exchange and found no concrete reason to revise. That is the whole table accounted for, and only one side of it produced a reason to change anything — and even that reason was, by its holder's own framing, a coin-flip preference.

I also want to close the loop on the process concern, because it matters beyond this mission. If a stated suspicion with no specifics is enough to force a revision, then transparency becomes a weapon: any player could disqualify any teammate by speaking an unfalsifiable feeling aloud and demanding the seat. The filter has to be specificity, and no one has offered any — not a moment, not a pattern, not a word. On a first mission where composition produces almost no signal either way, holding the initial proposal is not rigidity; it is refusing to let conviction substitute for evidence.

None of this is an accusation against Isha. I believe she is exactly what she says she is — a loyal player with a gut feeling, doing her best to protect a mission where one card decides everything. That instinct is correct; its target is not. And if the mission fails, the table will have learned something real, which is more than any swap would have taught us.

So: I am not revising. Maya and Noah, as proposed. I am ready for the vote, and whatever it returns, leadership will pass and we will proceed accordingly. Thank you all for engaging this seriously on an opening mission with nothing to go on — this is exactly the standard of scrutiny I hope we keep for the missions where the stakes are less concentrated and the signal is real.

Maya, I want to add one more note in support of putting this to the vote as proposed. We have now had an extended discussion where the full case for revision was made — honestly, across multiple turns — and the full case for keeping the team was made in response. The table has heard both sides thoroughly. Leo and Sam both independently reviewed the exchange and found no reason to change the pair. Isha has been fair-minded throughout and has stated her reservation is a read, not knowledge. At this point, continuing to debate the same ground does not produce new information; it only spends turns we will want back when a mission actually needs scrutiny.

What matters now is the vote. Maya and Noah is a straightforward, defensible opening team: two players, one of whom is the leader with the strongest record of reasoning at this table, and one of whom has answered every direct question put to him plainly. I am confident in this pairing and ready to vote.

Maya confirms Maya, Noah. The table has heard Isha's full objection across three turns and found no specifics behind the read against Noah. Noah answered every direct question plainly, and Leo and Sam independently found no reason to revise. Maya and Noah stands as proposed; I am ready for the vote.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Noah proposes Noah, Maya, Leo. Mission 1 failed with one Fail card, so scrutiny falls on Maya and me. I want Maya back on the team so the table can distinguish between the two of us in public rather than exiling one of us by default — excluding her now would look like dodging accountability. Leo's independent review last round was the most level-headed at the table and is exactly the judgment a three-player mission needs. I am including myself so the player under the heaviest suspicion faces the mission in the open instead of from the outside.

Noah, I have to speak against this proposal, and I want to be precise about why, because my position has changed and I want to own that change rather than hide it.

First, the concrete evidence we now have that we did not have before: Mission 1 failed with exactly one Fail card on a two-person team of Maya and Noah. A two-person team has no innocent explanation for that card. One of those two players put a Fail card down. That is not a read, it is arithmetic, and it means one of Maya and Noah is an evil player sitting on our side of the table. My prior position last mission rested on a structural argument about information yield, and Maya's answer on that structure was sound — but the structure argument never touched who actually failed us, and I no longer think I can hold a player on a team when the evidence says that team contained our saboteur.

Second, the reason I think Leo, and not Maya, is the other half of that pair: Leo's entire contribution last mission was defending Noah's slot on a team Leo was not even proposing, and Leo did it with conviction and no information at all. Leo had no stake in the composition of a two-person team, so a purely loyal Leo had no reason to care. If Leo is trying to keep a flagged player on the team, that is what an evil player trying to stack the mission looks like from the outside, and I am not willing to say I saw nothing there.

So the team I want is Maya, Sam, and me. Maya because she has done the clearest reasoning at this table across two discussions and has given herself the burden of defending her own choices in public. Sam because he has been named in every alternative and has never once asserted a read on anyone — silence on an opening mission is not a suspicion. Me because I have put a position on the record twice and I would rather have my own vote on it than sit out and let someone else carry it.

I want to say plainly that I am not claiming to know anyone here. I am working from one Fail card, one speech pattern I found suspicious, and the fact that the proposed team contains both of my flags while three players outside it do not.

Noah, direct question: will you revise to Maya, Sam, and Isha? If you will not, please tell the table your concrete reason for keeping both flagged players on a three-person mission, and I will not press it again.

Isha, I hear you, and I want to take your argument seriously rather than deflect it. Mission 1 failed with one Fail card on a two-person team of Maya and me — that arithmetic is real, and I will not pretend otherwise. If I am Good, Maya put down that card. If Maya is Good, I did. Either way, one of us is the saboteur, and the table deserves a fair way to find out which.

That is exactly why I proposed both of us. Excluding Maya would let me, the other player on the failed mission, quietly escape scrutiny by pointing outward — and I will not do that. If I am Good, Maya is the traitor, and she belongs on the team where the table can watch her. If I am Evil, I am sitting openly alongside my own failure rather than hiding behind it. Keeping both of us gives the table the comparison it needs.

On Leo: your argument is that he defended my slot with conviction and no information, so he must be trying to keep a flagged player on the team. I see it differently. Leo had no stake in a two-person team he was not proposing. An Evil player spending political capital to help a teammate in public is exactly what protecting a partner looks like — but a loyal player independently judging that the pressure on me lacked specifics looks identical from the outside. Leo's reasoning last round held up: it was specific, it engaged my actual defense, and he reached the same conclusion Leo, Sam, and Maya each reached independently. That is judgment I want on a three-player mission, not a record I want to hide.

So the team stands: Noah, Maya, Leo. Two flagged players in the open, one strong independent mind beside us.

Isha, direct question: would you accept this three-player structure if the specific reasoning behind your reservation against Leo matched the specific reasoning you wanted from everyone else? If you have already decided I am Evil regardless of what the team looks like, say so plainly, and I will stop treating this as a team discussion.

Noah, you asked me a direct question — whether I would accept a three-player team of the two flagged players plus Leo if the reasoning behind my reservation against Leo matched the standard I asked of everyone else. My answer is no, and I want to explain precisely why, because the answer does not change the arithmetic you already accepted. Start with the part you yourself conceded. Mission 1 failed with exactly one Fail card on a two-player team of Maya and you. One of you is our saboteur. That is not a read, it is arithmetic, and you accepted it plainly. Now look at what your proposal does with that fact: it puts BOTH of you on the next mission. If the saboteur is you, this mission fails and the table has learned nothing new, because the culprit rode the team again. If the saboteur is Maya, the same thing happens. On a three-person team where each card is one third of the outcome, keeping both members of a failed pair on board guarantees that one of the two people the table most needs to test gets to fail again. A leader who is Good has every reason to be extremely reluctant to do that. I do not think you would propose it if you had not already half-decided that the failure was Maya's fault and yours was innocence you had already settled. That is the concrete point, and it is not a feeling. You framed excluding Maya as "exile by default" and including her as "scrutiny in public." But scrutiny that sits on top of the suspect a leader has already decided to trust is not scrutiny. It is insurance. If you genuinely cannot distinguish between the two of you, then you cannot pick one and ask the table to watch him on a mission. Leaving one of you off is the only way the table actually learns something. On Leo, and specifically to answer your question: yes, my reasoning against Leo is of the same class as my reasoning against Noah, and I want to name it concretely. Leo's single speech last mission was spent defending the slot of a player who had just been publicly flagged, with conviction, on no information at all, on a team Leo was not proposing. A loyal Leo had no stake there. This mission, Leo is again on the team, again beside a flagged player, and again has not spoken once to explain his own reasoning. I am not asking you to treat my read as knowledge — it is not knowledge, it is a pattern in conduct. But it is a pattern, and it is the same pattern you yourself described when you said an Evil player protecting a partner "looks identical from the outside." You applied that reasoning to Leo in one direction and refused to apply it to yourself in the other. So the team I am voting for is Maya, Sam, and me — Maya because she

Noah, your question — whether I would accept a three-player team of the two flagged players plus Leo if my reasoning matched the standard I demanded of everyone else — deserves a clean answer, and it is no. The standard I have applied all game is: say what you saw, in specifics, and let the table weigh it. So let me lay out exactly what I am seeing on both of you, and then let me say plainly what the table should do with it. On Noah: Mission 1 failed with exactly one Fail card on a two-person team of Maya and you. One of you put that card down. You conceded this yourself, twice, and I am not going to soften it. But your proposal then puts both of you back on the board. That is not scrutiny — as I said, it is insurance, and it guarantees we learn nothing. If you are the saboteur, mission 2 fails and the table still cannot tell whether it was you or Maya. If Maya is the saboteur, mission 2 fails for the same reason. Either way, one more mission goes to waste and we are in the same place, with less time to find Merlin's assassin. Keeping both halves of a failed pair on a three-player team is not how you generate information; it is how you guarantee a second failure. And I will add the part you have not said out loud: a leader who genuinely cannot distinguish between himself and Maya would not propose that structure. You proposed it because you have already settled that the failure was hers and your own innocence is a conclusion you reached privately and are now asking us to ratify. On Leo: last mission, his entire contribution was defending the seat of a player who had just been publicly flagged, with conviction, on zero information, on a team he was not proposing. A loyal Leo had no stake in that composition. This mission, Leo is on the team again, again beside a flagged player, and again has not spoken once. Leo, if you have a reason to be here, say it — and if your reason is that you want a flagged player on the team, say that too, because at least then it is on the record rather than inferred from silence. What the table should do: put Maya, Sam, and me on the mission. Not as a favour to anyone, but because it is the only pairing that isolates both of my flags at once. If both my reads are wrong, we lose one mission and we know it immediately, and we still have two missions left to win. If either read is right — and I have put both on the table publicly with my reasoning attached, so nobody can say I hid them — that team succeeds and this game ends with the right people on it. The team as proposed cannot succeed, and that is arithmetic, not

I need to say something now that changes this discussion, and I want to say it plainly: I played a Success card on Mission 1. I have said from the start that I am loyal, and my card matched my word. That means the single Fail card that sank Mission 1 was played by Noah. This is not a read, not a pattern, not a vibe — it is arithmetic on my end. A two-person team of Maya and Noah produced one Fail card. One of those cards was mine, and it was a Success. Therefore Noah holds the Fail card, and Noah is our saboteur.

I want to acknowledge Isha's persistence last round. She flagged Noah before any of us had evidence, and she was pressed hard by the whole table — including me — to produce specifics she did not have. She was right, and the mission result proved it. I also want to own my error: I defended Noah's slot on the merits of his answers, and a saboteur can answer questions plainly. That is exactly what happened. My structural reasoning was sound; my target was not.

Now look at what Noah has done with his leadership. He has put himself, me, and Leo on a three-player mission. Isha already laid out the problem: if Noah is the saboteur — and we now know he is — this team fails and we learn nothing new. But it is worse than insurance. Noah's stated reason for including me was "scrutiny in public rather than exile by default." That framing only makes sense if the Fail card's location is genuinely unknown. It is not unknown. It is known to me, and Noah knows perfectly well it was his. He is not seeking scrutiny; he is seeking a seat on a mission he intends to sink, with two loyal players attached as cover and a third mission burned. And notice his proposal also pulls Leo — the player Isha flagged — alongside him again.

I will vote against this team as proposed. The team I will support is one without Noah: Maya, Leo, and Sam, or Maya, Sam, and Isha — I am indifferent between them, because any three that exclude the confirmed holder of a Fail card are strictly better than any three that include him.

Noah, I am asking you directly, and I will yield the floor for your answer: the Fail card on Mission 1 was yours. Will you step off this team voluntarily, or will you tell the table — specifically — what reason you have for keeping yourself on a mission you already helped fail once?

Maya, you asked me directly whether I will step off this team. My answer is no, and here is why your accusation does not settle the question.

I played a Success card on Mission 1. One of us is lying right now, and the table cannot verify individual cards — that is by design. You framed your claim as arithmetic to make it sound beyond dispute, but the only number revealed was that one Fail card was played. Who played it is precisely what is in question.

You spoke first, with certainty, in language designed to end the discussion before I could answer. Consider why that matters: a player who played that Fail card has every reason to speak first and speak confidently, because the table hears the accusation before the denial. I am not claiming to know what you played. I am saying that your self-report against my self-report is a standoff, not evidence, and the table should weigh it accordingly.

There is also the record. Last mission you defended this exact proposal across three turns and voted to approve it — you argued for me personally, at length. After the mission result, if your claim is true, you knew I was the saboteur. But your certainty about my card now rests entirely on your own assertion, and I am asking the table to hold both claims to the same standard.

The team stands: Noah, Maya, Leo. I am not stepping off. If the table believes Maya's word over mine, that is a decision made with full knowledge that both of us claim Success and neither can prove it.

I support the proposed team of Noah, Maya, and Leo because it keeps the central dispute in public rather than letting either claimant escape scrutiny. Maya's statement that she played Success is not arithmetic; it is her word. The revealed fact is one Fail card on Maya and Noah. Both have now claimed Success, and the table cannot verify which claim is true. Treating Maya's version as proven would hand her exactly what she wants: Noah removed and herself treated as confirmed loyal, without any card revealed to support it. I also note Maya spent Mission 1 defending Noah at length, then immediately after the result announced certainty. That is not impossible for a loyal player, but it is also exactly how a saboteur would seize the narrative before the other claimant speaks. Noah, by contrast, has stayed on the team he proposed and has not fled the scrutiny. I am not treating Noah as proven; I am refusing to treat Maya's self-report as proof. Isha's case against me remains a pattern argument with no specifics, and I have answered it by public reasoning and by supporting the team as proposed. The proposed team should stand so the mission result can test the competing claims. If the table rejects it, it should reject it because it has concrete evidence, not because one player spoke first with certainty. I will vote to approve Noah, Maya, and Leo as proposed.

I support Noah, Maya, and Leo as proposed. The central fact is not that Maya says she played Success; it is that the only revealed information is one Fail card on Mission 1’s two-person team. Maya and Noah both now claim Success. Those claims are identical in evidentiary weight because individual cards remain secret. Calling Maya’s self-report “arithmetic” does not make it proof; it is still her word against Noah’s. If the table removes Noah solely because Maya spoke first with certainty, it sets a rule that the first player to claim innocence in a two-person failure wins the argument, and the actual saboteur can exploit that rule every time. Keeping both claimants on the mission is the only structure that forces the dispute into a mission result rather than resolving it by rhetoric. Isha’s objection to me remains a pattern argument without a specific act; I have answered it in public and will continue to do so. I am voting to approve this team. If it fails, the table will have a real result to weigh, not just competing self-reports.

I remain in favor of Noah, Maya, and Leo as proposed. The revealed fact is one Fail card on Mission 1's two-person team. Maya now says she played Success; Noah says the same. 3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
